extracted.intended_audience: news publishers, editors, journalists, media researchers, and policy-makers
extracted.subtask_description: Synthesize and evaluate global trends in how audiences find, consume, trust, pay for, and respond to digital news, and the implications for publishers, platforms, and policy. Uses survey data, qualitative research, and country-level analysis across 47 markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust in news — key factors
rubrics_metrics.description: People want news to be accurate, fair, avoid sensationalism, be open about any agendas and biases including lack of diversity, own up to mistakes – and not pull punches when investigating the rich and powerful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four primary factors (accuracy, fairness, transparency about agendas/biases, accountability for mistakes) are strongly linked and consistent across countries, ages, and political viewpoints. They give a clear steer for publishers on how to build greater trust. Note caveat: transparency may matter less or even backfire for those already distrustful.

rubrics_metrics.name: User needs framework (User Needs 2.0)
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience user needs are nested in four basic needs of knowledge, understanding, feeling, and doing, operationalised as eight different needs (examples: 'update me', 'educate me', 'give me perspective', 'inspire', 'connect', 'entertain').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should assess both importance and perceived performance across these needs; audiences prioritize 'update me', 'educate me', and 'give me perspective'. The framework suggests outlets should supplement constant updating with more context, perspective, and occasional optimism to reduce avoidance and better serve gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: User Needs Priority Index (gap analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A metric combining the importance of each user need with the gap between importance and perceived media performance: percentage point gap × importance (as a decimal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this index to identify priority gaps (high importance but low perceived performance) — e.g., providing different perspectives and 'news that makes me feel better about the world' score highly on the priority index and indicate areas for editorial focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic use of AI and public comfort
rubrics_metrics.description: Public comfort varies by AI use: more comfortable with AI for behind-the-scenes tasks (transcription, translation, supporting journalists) and much less comfortable with AI-created content where AI is the primary author, especially for 'hard' news such as politics or war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings recommend proceeding with caution: keep humans 'in the driving seat', be transparent about AI use, avoid using AI to replace journalists on high-stakes topics, be aware of risks (hallucinations, copyright issues, synthetic media). Comfort correlates with trust in news and varies by country and topic seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable AI deployment principles for publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles: use AI to assist (e.g., transcription, summary, graphics), maintain human oversight for content creation, disclose when AI is used, and avoid deploying AI-generated content for sensitive topics without strong checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualitative findings: audiences want humans in control; misuse (or opaque use) of AI could rapidly erode trust. Some publishers deploy AI-generated bullet points or robot writers with limited oversight — these choices have reputational and legal risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gateways to news — platform mix and strategic implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Main gateways: search & aggregators (33%), social media (29%), direct (22%); mobile alerts and portals also significant. Platforms remain key but the mix is shifting and fragmenting across multiple networks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should recognise gateway differences by age and market (search valuable across ages; social/video more youth-centred), diversify traffic sources, and develop direct connections/subscription funnels because dependence on platform referrals increases vulnerability to platform strategy changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform reset and fragmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Attention is fragmenting: six networks now reach at least 10% of respondents (vs two a decade ago); Facebook news consumption is down globally; video-focused networks (YouTube, TikTok, Instagram Reels) are rising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'platform reset' means publishers face unpredictable referral flows and must adapt to formats prioritised by platforms (especially video). Track reach metrics over time and across markets to inform distribution strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift to video networks and short-form video consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Video is increasingly important, especially for younger groups: 66% access short news videos weekly; 51% access longer formats; 72% of news video consumption occurs on online platforms versus 22% on publisher websites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers face monetisation and connection challenges because most video consumption is on third-party platforms. Strategies must balance engaging video formats with efforts to retain audiences on owned channels; recognise market and age differences in video consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention sources: creators/influencers vs mainstream media
rubrics_metrics.description: On many platforms (Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok) alternative sources, influencers, and creators attract more attention than traditional news brands; on Facebook and X traditional brands/journalists still often lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure where audiences pay most attention by platform; methods can include asking respondents to name top mainstream and alternative accounts (as used in the report). Editorial and marketing responses may include partnerships with creators, adapting storytelling styles, or reinforcing brand distinctiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to distinguish trustworthy from untrustworthy content (platform-level)
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-reported ease/difficulty varies by platform: e.g., 27% of TikTok users say they struggle to detect trustworthy news (highest); 24% of X users report difficulty; around half of users of each network say they find it easy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These perceptions differ by country, political leaning, and age. Platforms have increased moderation and fact-checking but risks (and the potential flood of synthetic content) remain. Use platform-specific literacy efforts and verification units to address user confidence gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI-generated synthetic media and deepfake risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Increasing incidence of synthetic audio, images, and video (deepfakes) poses risks for elections and high-stakes reporting; qualitative research finds younger heavy social users often encounter them and expect detection to get harder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers and platforms should prepare technical and human defences, invest in verification, be transparent about checks, and warn audiences when synthetic content is suspected. Policy and moderation measures are also relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: News avoidance and fatigue metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Selective news avoidance is rising (39% sometimes/often avoid news, +3pp year-on-year); feelings of being 'overloaded' by news have grown substantially (+11pp since 2019). Reasons include repetitiveness, negativity, and the relentlessness of coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address avoidance by rebalancing coverage to include more context, perspective, and occasional optimism; use the user needs model to commission stories that 'educate', 'give perspective', or 'inspire' rather than only constant updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscription and payment behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Limited growth in news subscriptions: 17% paid for online news in a basket of 20 richer countries. High discounting observed (41% pay less than full price); 55% of non-payers say they'd pay nothing; only 2% of non-payers would pay a full-price subscription.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publisher strategies must recognise price sensitivity and 'winner-takes-most' dynamics where a few upmarket brands attract most subscribers. Building perceived value, reducing reliance on discounting, and targeting niches (podcasts, newsletters, local) can help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral and monetisation risk from platform changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Industry data show that changes in platform strategies reduced referrals last year — e.g., Facebook referrals to publishers fell by 48%, X by 27% — impacting traffic and monetisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor referral trends and platform product changes; diversify traffic sources; invest in direct channels, subscriptions, and first-party relationships to reduce exposure to sudden platform algorithmic shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust-building and transparency initiatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience interest in transparency (how news is checked/made) supports initiatives like the Trust Project and BBC Verify; audiences want to know 'how we know' as well as 'what we know.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement trust indicators, behind-the-scenes explanations, fact-checking transparency, and responsive units that explain verification methods. Note: transparency matters most to those who already trust news and less to the generally distrustful, so tailor communications accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience segmentation for product and editorial decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Demographic and political segmentation matters: younger groups favour video/short-form and different topics (inspiration, connection); older groups favour direct access and politics; gender differences in topic interest (men: politics/sport; women: health/wellness/environment); political leaning affects platform trust (e.g., left more suspicious of X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use segmentation to tailor formats, topics, and distribution: adapt tone and format for younger audiences, emphasise context/perspective for older/political audiences, and consider gendered topic preferences in commissioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic and local news gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences report gaps especially around local news (varies by country), health, education, environment, and mental health; sport and politics are often perceived as well served.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify underserved topics via surveys and user needs gap analysis; invest in coverage areas with unmet demand (local reporting, health, education) which can strengthen public service value and potentially drive engagement or subscriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audio and podcast strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Podcasts attract younger, well-educated, wealthier audiences; across 20 measured countries 35% accessed a podcast monthly and 13% accessed a news/current affairs podcast. Many podcasts are now filmed and distributed via video platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Podcasts can be a relatively low-cost format less dependent on platform algorithms. Strategies include building owned distribution, exclusives/windowing to drive direct traffic, and cross-posting to video platforms to increase discoverability.
